summary:
The Two-Faced Pacific is an interactive web application that helps people explore how changing Pacific Ocean conditions relate to water, vegetation, agriculture, and communities. Built for the Dancing with the SARs challenge, it combines real NASA–ISRO NISAR radar previews, NASA MODIS vegetation imagery, NOAA ocean-temperature records, and ERA5 weather estimates.

Users can compare dated radar images across seven study areas, follow monthly vegetation changes, and play a chronological concept globe driven by NOAA observations. Weather is shown as monthly anomalies against a 1991–2020 baseline, and source-linked news adds community context. Every view separates observed data from illustrations. The goal is to help students, educators, and communities ask better questions about environmental change, and to understand what satellite observations can and cannot show.
details:
The Two-Faced Pacific

Exploring Ocean–Land Connections through Radar, Vegetation, Weather, and Community Reporting

NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026 · Dancing with the SARs

Abstract

El Niño–Southern Oscillation (ENSO) links the tropical Pacific Ocean to rainfall and climate variability around the world, but its effects differ by place and season. This project asks: how can people use satellite observations and historical climate records to investigate environmental change in their own communities? We built an interactive web application that combines five data streams: NISAR radar previews, MODIS vegetation imagery, NOAA Niño 3.4 ocean records, ERA5 weather estimates, and source-linked news. The saved edition contains 88 dated radar frames across seven study areas, 21 monthly vegetation images, 97 weekly ocean observations, and 293 news records. Weather is expressed as monthly anomalies from a 1991–2020 baseline, so each month is compared with what is usual for that place and season. In October 2026, five of seven study locations show lower rainfall than their baseline and two show higher, and all seven show warmer temperatures. These are descriptive anomalies. The application is an exploration tool and does not claim that ENSO caused any local event.

1. Introduction

ENSO is a pattern of changing ocean temperatures and winds in the tropical Pacific. McPhaden, Zebiak, and Glantz (2006) describe it as an integrating concept that connects physical processes with societal consequences. This is the basis of our “two-faced” framing: one shared ocean can be associated with very different experiences on land. For example, parts of the western Pacific, such as the Philippines, often grow drier during El Niño, while parts of coastal Peru and Ecuador often grow wetter.

Satellite and climate data on these themes are public, but hard for students and communities to use. Radar images need explanation, vegetation indices need context, and weather data needs a baseline. This project places them side by side for the same place and period, with plain-language descriptions and clear limits.

2. Study Areas

Seven radar study areas were selected to cover both sides of the Pacific and different land and water settings:

•          Central Luzon, Philippines: rice-growing landscapes and irrigation

•          Angat reservoir, Philippines: reservoir shorelines, rainfall, and water management

•          Cagayan Valley, Philippines: agricultural landscapes and the Magat basin

•          Dadu, Pakistan: floodplain observations

•          Lower Piura, Peru: river and agricultural landscapes

•          Mekong Delta, Vietnam: agricultural and water-related seasonal patterns

•          Guayas–Babahoyo, Ecuador: floodplain and agricultural observations

3. Data3.1 Data inventory
  • NISAR radar: 88 dated radar frames across the seven study areas (for example, 12 saved dates for Angat). Source: Alaska Satellite Facility (ASF) catalog records and regional HH/HV browse images of the NISAR GCOV product, plus NASA GIBS daily mosaics.
  • MODIS vegetation: 21 monthly NDVI images within a 23-month calendar starting January 2025. Source: NASA GIBS layer MODIS_Terra_L3_NDVI_Monthly.
  • Ocean temperature: 97 weekly Niño 3.4 readings from 1 January 2025 to 4 November 2026, plus the seasonal Oceanic Niño Index. Source: NOAA Climate Prediction Center.
  • Weather: daily rainfall and maximum and minimum temperature for each study location, for 1991–2020 and for January 2025 onward. Source: ECMWF ERA5 through the Open-Meteo Historical Weather API.
  • News: 293 source-linked records from a supplied archive and GDELT discovery.
  • These counts describe available records. They are not field measurements or validated impacts.
3.2 Nature of each dataset
  • The NISAR images used here are browse previews. GIBS mosaics show radar backscatter in false color (ASF, n.d.-b). They are not calibrated measurements.
  • The underlying GCOV product contains calibrated, terrain-corrected radar measurements (ASF, n.d.-a). Our current workflow uses its catalog records and browse images only.
  • ERA5 combines observations with a numerical model to give a consistent historical reconstruction of the atmosphere (Hersbach et al., 2020). Values are gridded estimates at the selected coordinates, not weather-station readings.
  • The NOAA ocean indices are published by NOAA. We imported them and did not calculate them from satellite pixels.
4. Scientific Methods and Computations4.1 Monthly weather from daily ERA5 data

We requested daily precipitation and daily maximum and minimum air temperature for seven study locations. Daily temperature was approximated as the midpoint of the day’s maximum and minimum:

T_d = (Tmax_d + Tmin_d) / 2

Monthly temperature is the average of the daily values, and monthly precipitation is the sum of the daily values:

T_m = (1 / N_m) × Σ T_d, summed over d = 1 to N_m

P_m = Σ P_d, summed over d = 1 to N_m

N_m is the number of calendar days in the month. Temperature is in °C and precipitation is in millimetres. The temperature value is a monthly average of daily maximum–minimum midpoints. It is not an average of hourly temperatures.

4.2 Thirty-year baselines and anomalies

To account for normal seasonal differences, each month was compared with the same calendar month during 1991–2020. For example, October 2026 was compared with the average of the 30 Octobers from 1991 to 2020.

Baseline precipitation for month m = (1 / 30) × Σ P(y, m), summed over y = 1991 to 2020

Baseline temperature was calculated the same way. Anomalies are:

ΔP(y, m) = P(y, m) − baseline precipitation for month m

ΔT(y, m) = T(y, m) − baseline temperature for month m

A negative precipitation anomaly means less precipitation than the historical monthly baseline. A positive value means more.

Worked example, Angat, October 2026:

ΔP = 110.90 − 260.47 = −149.57 mm

ΔT = 27.89 − 26.84 = +1.05 °C

These are descriptive anomalies. They are not standardized drought indices or statistical significance tests, and they do not show that ENSO caused the differences.

4.3 Completeness checks and missing data

The pipeline compared the number of available daily values with the actual length of each calendar month, including leap years. A monthly precipitation total required a precipitation value for every day. A monthly temperature required a valid maximum–minimum pair for every day. Baselines required 30 complete years for the corresponding calendar month. Incomplete values stayed unavailable and were never replaced with zero or an estimate.

For example, the saved Angat record for November 2026 had 8 precipitation days and 7 temperature days out of 30 expected days, so its monthly values and anomalies are unavailable. This prevents a partly observed month from looking artificially dry just because the remaining days have not been recorded.

4.4 Aligning ocean observations with a selected month

The application imported NOAA’s weekly Niño 3.4 sea-surface temperatures and anomalies, and the separate seasonal Oceanic Niño Index (ONI). To match ocean context to a selected month, it picks the most recent weekly observation on or before that month’s final day:

t* = the latest weekly observation date t such that t ≤ end of month m

This prevents a later observation from describing an earlier month. It is a date-matching step, not a monthly average. Weekly Niño 3.4 anomalies and seasonal ONI values keep their different time scales and are not interchangeable.

The concept globe steps through the actual weekly observation dates and uses each week’s Niño 3.4 anomaly to drive illustrative colors and animation. Those spatial patterns are educational illustrations, not reconstructed rainfall or temperature.

4.5 NISAR acquisition screening and spatial overlap

The completed radar computation covers catalog searches, acquisition-date organization, footprint intersection, and metadata checks for candidate image comparisons. The fraction of a study bounding box covered by a radar acquisition footprint is:

C = Area(F ∩ B) / Area(B)

F is the acquisition footprint and B is the study bounding box. For example, one saved Central Luzon acquisition had C = 0.3256, or 32.56% of the bounding box. The calculation uses longitude–latitude polygon areas, so it is an approximate catalog-footprint overlap. It is not an equal-area ground measurement or an estimate of usable radar-pixel coverage.

Candidate pairs were also checked for matching acquisition and processing metadata. The saved Angat comparison pairs 23 June 2026 with 9 October 2026, both on track 140, frame 9, with provisional processing metadata.

These steps support choosing images for visual comparison. They do not establish a measured change in water area, soil moisture, or surface elevation. The project’s science-output status records calibrated GCOV processing and water-area validation as not yet available. Radar brightness also depends on viewing geometry, surface roughness, vegetation structure, and processing, so changes between dates support questions rather than conclusions.

4.6 Vegetation index

The vegetation timeline uses existing monthly MODIS NDVI imagery. The index is:

NDVI = (NIR − Red) / (NIR + Red)

NIR and Red are near-infrared and red reflectance. Healthy, dense vegetation reflects strongly in near-infrared and absorbs red, so higher NDVI generally means greener vegetation (Huete et al., 2002).

NASA’s processing system calculates this index. Our project retrieved and displayed the resulting imagery with NASA’s official GIBS color legend (Figure 6). It did not calculate NDVI from raw reflectance, did not produce site-average NDVI statistics, and did not estimate crop yield or classify vegetation damage. The timeline supports visual comparison across dates only.

4.7 News-headline sentiment

The supplied news archive was merged with GDELT results, duplicate normalized URLs were removed, and sentiment was calculated for 293 saved records using VADER (Hutto & Gilbert, 2014). VADER’s compound score is normalized as:

s = x / √(x² + 15)

x is the total sentiment after VADER’s lexical and grammatical rules. Scores range from −1 to +1.

Each headline received two scores: the original VADER score, and a climate-adjusted score in which eight potentially misleading terms, including “warming,” “positive,” “negative,” and “anomaly,” were set to neutral values. For one saved headline, the score changed from 0.3612 to 0.2263 after adjustment.

The adjustment is an exploratory method, not a separately validated sentiment model. Headline tone does not measure climate severity, public opinion, or whether an article is accurate. URL deduplication also does not remove syndicated stories published at different addresses.

4.8 Display calculations

To control illustrative graphics, rainfall anomalies are scaled by:

r = clip( ΔP / max(20, baseline precipitation), −1, +1 )

The denominator floor of 20 mm and the clipping to the range −1 to +1 keep unusually large values from causing extreme visual movement. This is a display calculation only. It is not a physical model of reservoir storage, soil moisture, or vegetation growth.

4.9 Software pipeline

Python scripts retrieve source records and imagery, organize them with per-site evidence files and image manifests, and package them for the application. The ASF Search library is used for NISAR catalog discovery. The interface uses React, TypeScript, and Vite, with Globe.gl, D3 Geo, TopoJSON, and MapLibre GL JS for visualization. Playwright and automated tests check navigation, date selection, missing-data handling, and interface behavior. A downloadable offline edition packages a smaller selection of real imagery and saved records. The code is released under the MIT license.

4.10 Scope of the completed analysis

The completed scientific work consists of historical aggregation, seasonal-baseline comparison, anomaly calculation, completeness checking, temporal alignment, spatial catalog screening, and exploratory text analysis. The project has not completed calibrated radar change measurements, validated flood or drought classification, causal attribution to ENSO, or predictive modeling.

5. System Overview

The application connects these data in five parts: Story (ocean–land links and how radar works), Sites (dated radar, comparison, and weather for one place), Globe (monthly vegetation playback and the concept globe), Media (source-linked reporting), and Data and method (provenance, comparison rules, and limits).

Figure 1. The Story page introduces the central question, “When the Pacific warms, what changes on land?”, and six chapters.Figure 2. Animated explainer of how a warm Pacific shifts rainfall. It is labeled “Animated explainer · Not measured data.”6. Results6.1 Weather anomalies, October 2026

Five locations (Central Luzon, Angat, Cagayan Valley, Dadu, and Mekong Delta) had less precipitation than their October baseline. Two (Lower Piura and Guayas–Babahoyo) had more. All seven were warmer than their baseline. This fits the contrast that motivates the project, with the Philippine sites drier and the Ecuador site wetter. It is a descriptive pattern for one month and does not show that ENSO caused it. Dadu and Lower Piura have very small October baselines (1.66 mm and 4.03 mm), so their anomalies are small in absolute terms. We report anomalies in millimetres and avoid percentages for this reason.

6.2 Radar evidence

Users can inspect dated NISAR previews for each study area and compare two dates side by side.

Figure 3. NISAR radar previews of Central Luzon on two saved dates, 23 June 2026 and 2 November 2026.Figure 4. Sites page for Angat reservoir with date controls and 12 saved image dates (frame 12 of 12, 2 November 2026).6.3 Vegetation

The “Land through time” view plays monthly MODIS NDVI imagery with site markers showing rainfall compared with the usual amount for that month.

Figure 5. Monthly vegetation playback (October 2026) with rainfall departures at study sites. The background globe is a 2004 NASA Blue Marble reference image and does not show the selected date.Figure 6. NASA’s NDVI color legend used in the application. Values run from 0.0 (browns, little or no vegetation) to 1.0 (dark green, dense vegetation).6.4 Ocean contextFigure 7. The concept globe, driven by weekly Niño 3.4 observations. The interface states that colors, towers, rings, and links show a concept, not measured temperature, rainfall, or local risk.6.5 Summary

The result is a working tool that lets a user move from the ocean–land explanation to a specific place and date, inspect dated radar, see vegetation and weather context for the same period, and follow each source link. It is not a new scientific finding. We have not run a formal user study and make no claim about educational effectiveness.

7. Limitations
  • The radar workflow uses catalog records and browse images. We have not done the calibrated pixel analysis needed to report water area or backscatter change.
  • Radar brightness changes with viewing geometry, surface roughness, vegetation structure, and processing. Reservoir operations, irrigation, planting, and harvest can also explain changes.
  • Our data does not show that ENSO caused any particular local event. We do not report validated crop loss, reservoir volume, landslides, or flood extent.
  • ERA5 values are model-based estimates at a point, not station measurements. Anomalies are descriptive and are not drought indices or significance tests.
  • Headline scores describe language only, and the climate-term adjustment has not been separately validated.
  • Seven study areas and a record of about two years are not enough to establish ENSO relationships statistically.
8. Future Work

A rigorous extension would process compatible calibrated GCOV acquisitions, convert backscatter to decibels (dB = 10 × log10 of the calibrated value), apply valid-pixel masks and quality controls, and compare results with independent gauges, field observations, and agricultural records. We would also compare weather anomalies with ONI phases over a longer record, compute site-average NDVI statistics, and run a user study with students and educators.

9. Originality and Impact

The contribution is an accessible link between satellite evidence, historical context, and questions people recognize: changing shorelines, farming seasons, rainfall, and community experience. It is meant for students, educators, community organizations, and people new to Earth-observation data.
